elements.quote: Human studies published in English were assessed for eligibility against the following criteria: Population: older children and adults who survived an episode of documented severe malnutrition in LMICs or famine exposure in childhood and adolescence (defined as 0-18 years of age). Exposure: exposure definitions included two closely related groups: (1) documented severe malnutrition in childhood ... or (2) famine conditions ... Outcomes: a range of cardiometabolic NCD outcomes ... was considered if they were based on an objective clinical outcome measured at least 1 year after exposure to severe malnutrition or famine. All study designs were eligible.
elements.reason: Specifies population, exposure, eligible study designs (all designs), and follow-up timing for outcomes (objective clinical outcome measured at least 1 year after exposure). However, settings are not explicitly specified, and there is no explicit statement of all question-framework components (e.g., follow-up requirements beyond the 1-year outcome timing).

elements.quote: Human studies published in English were assessed for eligibility against the following criteria: ... Grey literature and unpublished studies were excluded.
elements.reason: Language (English) and publication/report status exclusion (grey literature and unpublished studies) are stated. Dissemination year is not specified in the retrieved evidence.
No evidence is provided that the review distinguishes exclusions due to (i) outcomes not measured versus (ii) outcome results not reported.

elements.quote: Data from studies of famine survivors and documented severe childhood malnutrition were analysed separately to account for the different nature of the exposures.
elements.reason: The review specifies groups used for analysis/synthesis at least at the exposure level (famine survivors vs documented severe childhood malnutrition). However, the retrieved evidence does not show how these groups are explicitly linked to the specific comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.reason: A rationale is provided for a notable eligibility restriction (excluding studies of stunted children alone). Other notable restrictions mentioned (e.g., exclusion of grey literature/unpublished studies) do not include rationales in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Our results build on a narrative review of differences in cardiometabolic risk between marasmus and kwashiorkor survivors from Boyne et al (2017) by systematically identifying new evidence for an effect of severe malnutrition and famine exposure in childhood on NCD risk. 11 Building on the DOHaD hypothesis, these findings indicate that severe childhood malnutrition may not only have serious implications for short-­ term morbidity and mortality but also for survivors' long-­ term health. This concept is described by Wells' (2018) 'capacity-­ load model of NCD risk', which proposes that individuals develop physiological traits during early life that give them the capacity to maintain homeostasis in metabolism and cardiovascular function when challenged by a metabolic load. 66
elements.reason: The discussion interprets the results by explicitly relating them to prior evidence (Boyne et al 2017 narrative review), theory (DOHaD hypothesis), and a named model (Wells 2018 capacity-load model).

elements.quote:
We acknowledge several limitations. Due to our broad scope, there was extensive clinical and methodological heterogeneity between studies, rendering it difficult to directly compare study findings. As all studies were observational, associations cannot be interpreted as causal. This makes it difficult to disentangle the effects of fetal and postnatal malnutrition. Few studies controlled for effects of foetal malnutrition as the proxy measure of birth weight was rarely available; however, four studies showed independent effects of postnatal malnutrition on NCD risk after controlling for birth weight. 22 42 52 53 Inadequately controlled age effects are another important confounder...

Without an age-­ matched or age-­ balanced control group, age differences between groups may explain many of the effects on NCD outcomes attributed to famine exposure...

Another limitation is the small sample size in some studies; thus, the children included may not represent the wider affected/at-­ risk population and chance observations are possible. We also note the risk of selection and information bias. Because severe childhood malnutrition is associated with high mortality, participants may represent the healthiest survivors and any effects observed in these populations may underestimate long-­ term health impacts of severe malnutrition. 9 93 Misclassification of famine exposure status is an important source of information bias...

Finally, we recognise the currently limited data sources on this topic; although we identified an important number of individual papers, many were from the same famine event and some had high risk of bias.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly states multiple limitations of the included evidence, covering heterogeneity, observational design (non-causal inference), confounding (fetal/postnatal and age effects), small sample size, selection/information bias, exposure misclassification, and limited/high-risk-of-bias data sources.
